```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(deconflate)
```

Inputs are three tables: the diseases, their associations and one impact
table. Each table can be a CSV file
(with any name) or a data frame typed in R. `cm_read_inputs()` checks every
table, reports all problems at once, and returns a model (`cm_model()`) that
`deconflate()` adjusts.

## The tables

Each table is a named argument of `cm_read_inputs()`:

| Argument | Contents | Required columns |
|---|---|---|
| `diseases` | one row per disease | `disease`, `value` |
| `associations` | association estimates, one row per estimate | `disease`, `associated_with`, `value` |
| `impacts` | the raw impact estimates of one outcome, one row per estimate | `disease`, `value` |

`diseases` and `impacts` are required. `deconflate()` also needs at least
one association; without any, `cm_sensitivity()` and `cm_threshold()`
show how much associations could matter. The optional columns are
described in `?cm_read_inputs`:

* `diseases`: `measure` (`prevalence` (default), `probability` or
  `incidence_rate`);
* `associations`: `among`, `adjusted_for`, `measure` (`OR` (default),
  `RR`, `RD`, `phi`, `prevalence` or `OR_ratio`), `study`;
* `impacts`: `among`, `adjusted_for`, `study`, and one `label` and one
  `units` per table; a `measure` column makes them event impacts (see
  below).

Every table can also have a `note` column for free text (for example the
source of a value; the package never uses it), and the columns `dist` and
`p1`-`p4` for uncertain values (see Uncertainty below). Column names are
not case-sensitive. Prevalences, probabilities, associations, impacts and
the overall risk must all refer to the same period (for example a
lactation or a year) and the same population.

A row is about a disease or a combination of diseases (ids separated by
`";"`), holds in the whole population or within a subgroup (`among`: a
disease, `"no "` and a disease, or `"no others"`), and is crude unless
`adjusted_for` names other diseases (ids separated by `";"`, or `"all"`).
Several rows can describe the same thing, e.g. estimates from several
studies. `?cm_associations` and `?cm_impacts` define every kind of row;
`vignette("interactions")` shows them at work.

Every disease needs a row of its own in the impact table (use 0 for no
impact). Additive impacts can be in any units, the same for every row;
results come back in those units.

## Start from the template

`cm_template()` writes an example set of files to a folder:

```{r}
dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "my-inputs")
cm_template(dir, overwrite = TRUE)
list.files(dir)
read.csv(file.path(dir, "yield.csv"))
```

The files are three diseases (`diseases.csv`), their odds ratios
(`associations.csv`), additive impacts on milk yield in percent
(`yield.csv`) and event impacts on culling (`culling.csv`, see below).
Rename them, or add files for other outcomes, as you like: the file names
carry no meaning.

## Read the files

Pass each file to its argument:

```{r}
yield <- cm_read_inputs(
  diseases = file.path(dir, "diseases.csv"),
  associations = file.path(dir, "associations.csv"),
  impacts = file.path(dir, "yield.csv")
)
yield
deconflate(yield, n_draws = 0)
```

Some values in the template have a distribution,
so `deconflate()` would by default also run 1000 draws for intervals;
`n_draws = 0` gives point estimates only (see Uncertainty below).

## Associations

### Unknown pairs and odds ratios of 1

A pair of diseases that no association row mentions is **unknown**.
`deconflate()` fills in its association from the other associations (the
maximum-entropy distribution of disease combinations), and lists it in
`$unknown_pairs`. To state that two diseases are unrelated, give the pair an
odds ratio of 1 (with no distribution).

Here the MET:SCK row is left out:

```{r}
a <- read.csv(file.path(dir, "associations.csv"))
a[, c("disease", "associated_with", "value", "measure")]
y_unknown <- cm_read_inputs(diseases = file.path(dir, "diseases.csv"),
                            associations = a[-2, ],
                            impacts = file.path(dir, "yield.csv"))
y_unknown
r_unknown <- deconflate(y_unknown, n_draws = 0)
r_unknown
r_unknown$unknown_pairs
```

`$unknown_pairs` lists the pairs without an association and the odds ratio
the fit gave them. With an odds ratio of 1 for MET:SCK instead, every pair
has an association, and the pairwise tables are used directly:

```{r}
a_indep <- a
a_indep$value[2] <- 1
y_indep <- cm_read_inputs(diseases = file.path(dir, "diseases.csv"),
                          associations = a_indep,
                          impacts = file.path(dir, "yield.csv"))
deconflate(y_indep, n_draws = 0)
```

The two are different statements: an unknown pair is filled in from the
other associations, while an odds ratio of 1 is an estimate of no
association. Some published analyses treated unlisted pairs as independent;
to do the same, add those pairs with an odds ratio of 1.

### Measures

The measures are `OR` (default), `RR`, `RD`, `phi`, `prevalence` (the
prevalence of `disease` among animals with `associated_with`, or within
`among`) and `OR_ratio` (how much a third disease, in `among`, changes an
odds ratio). Files written for earlier versions may use the columns
`disease1` and `disease2`, the measures `cond_prob`, `unknown`,
`independent` or `table`, the count columns `n11`, `n10`, `n01` and `n00`,
or a separate three-way or interactions table; these are reported with
what to do instead:

```{r}
cm_check_inputs(
  diseases = data.frame(disease = c("d1", "d2", "d3"), value = c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20)),
  associations = data.frame(disease = c("d1", "d1", "d2"), associated_with = c("d2", "d3", "d3"),
                            value = c(0.3, 1, NA), measure = c("cond_prob", "independent", "table")),
  impacts = data.frame(disease = c("d1", "d2", "d3"), value = c(2.5, 5, 7.5))
)
```

For a study's 2x2 table, compute the odds ratio yourself, `n11 * n00 /
(n10 * n01)` (both diseases, only the first, only the second, neither), and
enter it with measure `OR`. If a cell is zero, decide how to handle it (e.g.
add 0.5 to every cell) before computing the odds ratio.

### Adjusted odds ratios

An odds ratio from a logistic regression that included other diseases of
the model is entered with those diseases in `adjusted_for`; the model
matches it as the regression coefficient it is, not as a crude odds ratio.
Covariates that are not diseases of the model (parity, herd, ...) cannot be
matched: they are noted, and the row is used as a crude odds ratio, which is
an approximation:

```{r}
d12 <- cm_diseases(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20))
a_adj <- cm_associations(c("d1", "d1", "d2"), c("d2", "d3", "d3"), c(1.8, 1.2, 2.5),
                         adjusted_for = c("d3; parity; herd", NA, NA))
r_adj <- deconflate(cm_model(d12, cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(2.5, 5, 7.5)),
                             associations = a_adj), n_draws = 0)
r_adj$notes
```

### Several rows for one item

Two studies of the same odds ratio are two rows; they are pooled (random
effects by default, see `?deconflate`). Several impact rows of one disease
(e.g. a crude and an adjusted estimate) are fitted together by weighted
least squares. The five-disease example below has both;
`$heterogeneity` reports how well the rows agree.

## Several outcomes

An impact table holds one outcome, and `deconflate()` adjusts one impact
table per call. For several outcomes, keep one impact table per outcome and
repeat the call; the disease and association tables are shared. The
installed folder `five_diseases` has impact tables for milk yield (in
percent) and calving interval (in days), among others:

```{r}
five <- system.file("extdata", "five_diseases", package = "deconflate")
list.files(five)
outcomes <- c(yield = "impacts_yield.csv", calving_interval = "impacts_calving_interval.csv")
results <- lapply(outcomes, function(f) {
  m <- cm_read_inputs(diseases = file.path(five, "diseases.csv"),
                      associations = file.path(five, "associations.csv"),
                      impacts = file.path(five, f))
  deconflate(m, n_draws = 0)
})
results$calving_interval
```

The results can then be combined in base R, e.g. into one long table:

```{r}
do.call(rbind, lapply(names(results), function(o) {
  data.frame(outcome = o, units = results[[o]]$units,
             results[[o]]$adjusted[, c("disease", "rows", "adjusted")])
}))
```

## Event impacts

Impacts on an event such as culling or death are event impacts: hazard
ratios, rate ratios, risk ratios, odds ratios or risk differences. Their
table has a `measure` column (`HR`, `rate_ratio`, `RR`, `OR` or `RD`, which
can be mixed); rows are crude or adjusted (`adjusted_for`), about diseases or
combinations, as for additive impacts. They are adjusted with
`event_model = TRUE`, which needs the overall risk of the event in the
population over the period; risk ratios, odds ratios and risk differences
must refer to the same period. The template's `culling.csv`:

```{r}
read.csv(file.path(dir, "culling.csv"))[, c("disease", "adjusted_for", "measure", "value")]
culling <- cm_read_inputs(diseases = file.path(dir, "diseases.csv"),
                          associations = file.path(dir, "associations.csv"),
                          impacts = file.path(dir, "culling.csv"))
deconflate(culling, event_model = TRUE, overall_risk = 0.25, n_draws = 0)
```

The adjusted hazard ratios are each disease's own effect; the result also
gives the risk attributable to disease and its split by disease. If an
adjusted hazard ratio falls on the other side of 1 from its raw estimate,
`deconflate()` warns: the raw estimate is weaker than the disease's
associations alone would produce, so check the estimate and its source
population.

A table with a `measure` column needs `event_model = TRUE`, and
`event_model = TRUE` needs a `measure` column:

```{r}
tryCatch(deconflate(culling, n_draws = 0), deconflate_unsupported = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

See `vignette("event-impacts")` for the model and its results.

## Uncertainty

There is no separate uncertainty file: an uncertain value gets its
distribution in its own row, in the columns `dist` and `p1`-`p4`, so point
values and uncertain values sit side by side. A row with an empty `dist` is
a point value. In the template, the LAM prevalence, the LAM:SCK odds ratio
and two yield impacts have a distribution:

```{r}
read.csv(file.path(dir, "diseases.csv"))[, c("disease", "measure", "value", "dist", "p1", "p2")]
read.csv(file.path(dir, "associations.csv"))[, c("disease", "associated_with", "value", "dist", "p1", "p2", "p3")]
```

`cm_read_inputs()` keeps them in the model, and `deconflate()` draws them
(1000 draws by default) and adds 95% intervals to the results:

```{r}
deconflate(yield, n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
```

The central estimate always uses the point values (`value`); the draws give
the intervals. Values are drawn on the scale they were entered on:

* a disease's `value` (e.g. a prevalence or an incidence rate);
* an association row's `value`, on its own measure (e.g. an odds ratio);
* an impact row's `value`, in the units of its table (for event impacts, on
  the scale of the measure, e.g. a hazard ratio).

`dist` and the parameters `p1`-`p4`:

| `dist` | `p1` | `p2` | `p3` | `p4` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fixed` | value | | | |
| `normal` | mean | sd | lower bound (optional) | upper bound (optional) |
| `lognormal` | meanlog | sdlog | | |
| `lognormal_ci` | estimate | lower CI | upper CI | level (default 0.95) |
| `beta` | shape1 | shape2 | min (default 0) | max (default 1) |
| `pert` | min | mode | max | lambda (default 4) |
| `pert_mean` | min | mean | max | lambda (default 4) |
| `uniform` | min | max | | |

The checks report a distribution with missing or invalid parameters and
parameters without a `dist`; a point value outside its distribution's
range is noted. In the model, the distributions are kept in
`$distributions`, keyed `prob:<disease>`, `associations:<row>` and
`impacts:<row>` (rows numbered from 1 in each table), the same keys as
`cm_model(distributions = )`, which also accepts `assoc:<d1>:<d2>` and
`impact:<disease>` when they name one row:

```{r}
names(yield$distributions)
```

See `vignette("uncertainty")` for the draws, their intervals and rejected
draws.

## When something is wrong

All problems are listed with their table, row (counting from the first row
below the header) and column, so that they can be fixed in one pass.
`cm_check_inputs()` returns them without stopping:

```{r}
cm_check_inputs(
  diseases = data.frame(disease = c("LAM", "SCK", "SCK"), value = c(0.25, 1.4, 0.3)),
  associations = data.frame(disease = "LAM", associated_with = "MET", value = 2.0),
  impacts = data.frame(disease = c("LAM", "SCK"), value = c("4.81", "8,40"))
)
```

`cm_read_inputs()` stops with the same list (an error of class
`deconflate_input_problems`) when there are errors, and prints notes
otherwise.

The installed folder `example_with_errors` has a disease table, an
association table, an additive impact table (`impacts_yield.csv`) and an
event impact table (`culling.csv`), each with mistakes explained in its
`note` column: a missing distribution parameter, a prevalence above 1, a
duplicate disease, a combination in the disease table, a missing
association value, an unknown disease, an odds ratio adjusted only for
factors outside the model, measures from earlier versions, rows that are
not well formed (a subgroup naming the row's own disease, an adjusted risk
ratio, an `OR_ratio` without a subgroup), a decimal comma, two units in one
table, an unsupported distribution, and a point value outside its
distribution:

```{r}
err <- system.file("extdata", "example_with_errors", package = "deconflate")
list.files(err)
cm_check_inputs(diseases = file.path(err, "diseases.csv"),
                associations = file.path(err, "associations.csv"),
                impacts = file.path(err, "impacts_yield.csv"))
```

The event impact table has the `estimand` column of earlier versions (now
ignored, with a note), a row without a measure, a hazard ratio of 0 and a
risk difference above 1 (the disease table's problems, listed above, are
left out here):

```{r}
p <- cm_check_inputs(diseases = file.path(err, "diseases.csv"),
                     impacts = file.path(err, "culling.csv"))
p[p$table == "impacts", ]
```

## When adjusted impacts change sign

An adjusted impact on the other side of zero from its raw impact (a disease
that seems to raise yield once its associated diseases are accounted for),
or one that has almost vanished, usually means that the inputs contradict
each other under the model: the raw impact is smaller than what the
diseases that come with it account for. `deconflate()` warns about sign
changes. With `diagnose = TRUE`, it also shows which inputs drive them.

As an example, take the five-disease yield table with a raw SCK impact of
1.0 instead of 2.5:

```{r}
five <- system.file("extdata", "five_diseases", package = "deconflate")
low <- cm_read_inputs(diseases = file.path(five, "diseases.csv"),
                      associations = file.path(five, "associations.csv"),
                      impacts = file.path(five, "impacts_yield.csv"))
low$impacts$value[low$impacts$disease == "SCK"] <- 1.0
res <- deconflate(low, n_draws = 0, diagnose = TRUE)
res$problems
```

How to read it:

* SCK is flagged: its adjusted impact is below zero. A disease is also
  flagged when its adjusted impact has shrunk by more than 90%.
* Each input with a distribution gets the change in the flagged impact when
  it moves up by one SD of its own uncertainty. The MAS-SCK prevalence row
  (the share of SCK cows with MAS) lowers SCK's adjusted impact by about
  0.19 per SD; on its own, a value 1.5 SD lower would remove the flag (the
  flag goes when the adjusted impact reaches 10% of the raw impact). The
  effects are in the impact's own units for every kind of input, so
  prevalences, associations and impacts can be compared directly.
* An input without a distribution gets the value at which the flag
  disappears instead: here SCK's own raw impact would have to be about 1.3.
* A flagged impact that no single input fixes (within 3 SD, or within a
  quarter to three times the value of an input without a distribution)
  points to several inputs together, or to a structural problem such as
  units.

The listed inputs are worth checking, not necessarily wrong. Common causes:

* units or measurement windows that differ between tables (kg vs %, a
  305-day yield vs a test-day yield);
* estimates that measure different things. A study of "cows with the
  disease alone vs healthy cows" estimates something close to the disease's
  own impact, so it belongs in a row with `among = "no others"`, not in a
  crude row; an estimate from a regression adjusted for other diseases
  belongs in a row with `adjusted_for`. Pooling such estimates into one
  crude value before entering it mixes them up. Enter them as separate
  rows instead (see "Several rows for one item" above);
* source populations with different comorbidity patterns.

Setting a negative adjusted impact to zero does not fix it: the
contradiction stays in the inputs and in the other adjusted impacts.

The check also lists rows that disagree with other rows for the same
quantity (a standardised residual of 2 or more), with what changes without
each. Here the crude MAS row of the calving-interval table is changed from
9 to 20 days:

```{r}
ci <- cm_read_inputs(diseases = file.path(five, "diseases.csv"),
                     associations = file.path(five, "associations.csv"),
                     impacts = file.path(five, "impacts_calving_interval.csv"))
ci$impacts$value[3] <- 20
deconflate(ci, n_draws = 0, diagnose = TRUE)$problems
```

The check reruns the central estimate about twice for every input with a
distribution and a few times for every input without one, so it takes
longer than `deconflate()` itself (a few minutes for the twelve diseases of
the 2024 global dairy example). It does not change the results.

## Tables typed in R

Any table can be a data frame instead of a file, with the same columns,
including the distribution columns:

```{r}
typed <- cm_read_inputs(
  diseases = data.frame(disease = c("d1", "d2", "d3"), value = c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20)),
  associations = data.frame(disease = c("d1", "d2"), associated_with = c("d2", "d3"),
                            value = c(2, 3), measure = "OR",
                            dist = c("lognormal_ci", NA), p1 = c(2, NA), p2 = c(1.4, NA),
                            p3 = c(2.9, NA)),
  impacts = data.frame(disease = c("d1", "d2", "d3"), value = c(2.5, 5, 7.5),
                       units = "% of yield", dist = c("normal", NA, NA),
                       p1 = c(2.5, NA, NA), p2 = c(0.5, NA, NA))
)
typed
deconflate(typed, n_draws = 0)$adjusted
```

Here the pair d1:d3 has no row, so it is unknown and filled in by the fit.
The R constructors (`cm_diseases()`, `cm_associations()`,
`cm_population()`, `cm_impacts()`, `cm_model()`) build the same model
directly.

## Disease ids

Ids are used in keys such as `assoc:d1:d2` and in lists such as `"d1; d2"`,
so they must not contain `|`, `;` or `:`, nor leading or trailing spaces.
`"all"` and `"others"` are reserved, and an id cannot start with `"no "`
(these are used in `adjusted_for` and `among`):

```{r}
tryCatch(cm_diseases(c("LAM", "SCK:early"), c(0.25, 0.40)),
         deconflate_error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
tryCatch(cm_diseases(c("LAM", "all"), c(0.25, 0.40)),
         deconflate_error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

## Fuller examples

The folder `five_diseases` uses every feature on five diseases: all
probability types and association measures, two studies of one odds ratio
(pooled), an `OR_ratio` row, crude, adjusted and subgroup impact rows,
several rows for one disease, interactions (in `impacts_welfare.csv`), event
impacts with mixed measures and an interaction (`culling.csv`), and every
distribution type mixed with point values. Its `run_all_features.R` script
runs every part of the package on it.

The folder `global_dairy_2024` holds the inputs of Rasmussen et al. (2024)
for 12 diseases: `diseases.csv`, `associations.csv` (the 38 odds ratios of
Table 3), `impacts_yield.csv`, `impacts_fertility.csv` and `culling.csv`
(hazard ratios entered as crude rows), with the input distributions of
the paper's analysis in the `dist` columns. Pairs not in Table 3 have no row,
so they are unknown:

```{r}
gd <- system.file("extdata", "global_dairy_2024", package = "deconflate")
cm_read_inputs(diseases = file.path(gd, "diseases.csv"),
               associations = file.path(gd, "associations.csv"),
               impacts = file.path(gd, "impacts_yield.csv"))
```

`example_global_dairy()` returns the same inputs as a model. (The published
analysis treated these pairs as independent.)
